rashi:a1.1: What, is it not referring to the animal: the clause that teaches “they penalize him” means that we penalize him to redeem the animal. So [the baraita speaks of one who] sold the animal for its fetuses, since receivership is only for the fetuses, and we penalize him according to both Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis, for the Rabbis disagree with Rabbi Yehuda only with regard to firstborn status.
rashi:a1.2: No, to the fetus: we penalize him because it was already in her womb and he sold it outright; but fetuses she will conceive in the future do not concern us.
rashi:a2.1: The language is also precise: that it refers to the fetus, since it teaches “he gives all its value to the priest.” If it referred to the animal, what business would the priest have with it?
rashi:a3.1: Supports him: the clause that teaches “they penalize.”
rashi:a4.1: Or not specifically: meaning we do not penalize him that much. Alternatively, we penalize him even more than this if the gentile will not agree [to sell it back] for that.
rashi:a4.2: Come and hear: since for a slave it teaches one hundred and here ten, conclude that it is meant specifically; for if not, let it teach one hundred in both or ten in both. [The answer:] Actually, for an animal it is not specific, since we do not penalize him that much; but for a slave, because each and every day, etc.
rashi:a4.3: Specifically: one hundred, or not specifically. In the latter version we read for a slave “up to ten times its value.” So the hundred said of an animal is not specific, since for a slave, whom [the gentile] keeps from his mitzvot, we penalize only ten.
rashi:a4.4: A slave is different: that is why we do not penalize him more, because when he redeems him the slave does not return to his master, as we hold in tractate Gittin (43b): one who sells his slave to a gentile, the slave goes free.
rashi:a8.1: And he challenges: in the case of an animal, what is the reason we penalize him more? Because it returns to him.
rashi:a8.2: This is the reading: “If so, let him be penalized one more.” Beyond ten he should be penalized only the amount of its value, since in that it returns to him he gains only its value, and the fine itself is only ten. So let it teach eleven times its value, and no more.
rashi:a9.1: All the firstborn: among Israel. The Rabbis hold that had it written only “firstborn among Israel,” it would mean that even part of a firstborn belonging to an Israelite is obligated in firstborn status.
rashi:a11.1: Comes to fill: [it is not obligated] until all of it belongs to the Israelite.
rashi:a11.2: To detract: for “all” [kol] means any amount at all, as in “Your maidservant has nothing [kol] in the house” (II Kings 4:2).
rashi:a12.1: Even its ear: even if the gentile’s partnership is only in the firstborn’s ear, it is not sacred.
rashi:a12.2: And let him say to him: the priest, to the gentile.
rashi:a12.3: Take your ear and go: for even [as] a blemished firstborn, it is given to the priest.
rashi:a13.1: A carcass: for example, where the gentile has a share in its gullet or its windpipe. Since its life is in the gentile’s hand, it is considered as though all of it belonged to the gentile.
rashi:a13.2: A tereifa: for example, [a share in the leg] from the knee joint upward.
rashi:a14.1: With regard to what do they disagree: Rav Ḥisda and Rava.
rashi:a14.2: Rava holds that a tereifa cannot live: therefore it is as though all of it belonged to the gentile.
rashi:a14.3: And Rav Ḥisda holds that a tereifa can live: therefore only an item that renders it a carcass counts.
rashi:a15.1: Do not disagree: Rav Ḥisda and Rava do not disagree with Rav Huna; but Rav Ḥisda and Rava do disagree [with each other].
rashi:a15.2: This, to it: if the gentile has a share in the firstborn itself, even in its ear, it is not sacred.
rashi:a15.3: To its mother: either [an item that renders it] a carcass or [one that renders it] a tereifa.
rashi:a16.1: “From all your livestock you shall take the males [tizakher]”: if all the livestock is yours, then tizakher: if there is a male of yours, you shall consecrate it, as we translate [in the Targum]: “the males you shall consecrate.”
rashi:a17.1: Objects to this: to all of them.
rashi:a17.2: Sheger behema, sheger be-vehema: it dwells in the animal’s womb when its time to emerge has not yet come. Another version: sheger behema, what the animal casts off and miscarries. So even though they are not viable, they are sacred. Here too, even if the gentile had in it an item that renders it a carcass, let the Israelite’s share be sacred, even though it is not viable.
tosafot:a10.1: In brief: And Rabbi Yehuda holds that “firstborn” implies the whole firstborn. This is difficult: in chapter Kisui HaDam (Ḥullin 88a) it is said the other way around: Rabbi Yehuda says “its blood” means part of its blood, and the Rabbis hold all its blood. Rabbeinu Tam explained that there, because “blood” alone means all the blood, the Torah wrote “its blood” to mean part of its blood, just as here it wrote “all” to mean even any amount. But that is difficult, since there Rabbi Yehuda expounds “its blood” for a different purpose. Further, Rabbeinu Tam ruled like Rabbi Yehuda there (see Tosafot, Gittin 7b), and that clashes with our passage, where the halakha is not like Rabbi Yehuda, as it says below (3b): “No one is concerned with this ruling of Rabbi Yehuda, who says partnership with a gentile is obligated.” So one may explain instead that we compare only what the Gemara itself compares: “a virgin, even part of virginity” (Yevamot 59a), which Ketubot 97b compares to the dispute over whether part of the money is like all of the money. Those two are alike: when virginity was diminished and part remains, it is as though all remained; when part of the ketuba money remains, she has sustenance as though all remained. But there are many derashot that cannot be equated: “a sheep, even part of a sheep,” disputed by Rabbi Elazar and the Rabbis (Ḥullin 79b, 132a), and the dispute of Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira and the Rabbis over “all souls.” And even if we did equate “its blood” with our case, there is no difficulty that here the ruling is not like Rabbi Yehuda while there it says no one is concerned with Rabbi Shimon’s view that we do not say part of the money is like all of it; on the contrary, that supports ruling like the Rabbis, since without “all,” “firstborn” would imply part of a firstborn, and there too “virgin” implies part of virginity. Another answer, so that Rabbi Yehuda does not contradict himself: the plain verse speaks of an ordinary animal, owned entirely by its Jewish owners with no gentile partnership, so without “all” we would apply it to a whole firstborn. Or: because it is written “every firstborn among Israel” (Numbers 3:13), and “among Israel” implies all of it, as said in Yevamot 102a regarding ḥalitza, [which applies only] when both father and mother are Israelites; but elsewhere [the word] may well imply part. tosafot:a13.1: Rav Ḥisda says an item that renders it a carcass; Rava says an item that renders it a tereifa: in the first chapter of Temura (11b), regarding one who says “the foot of this one is a burnt offering,” the reading is reversed. This is one of the reversed readings, and the one there is primary: Rav Ḥisda says Rabbi Yehuda concedes in the case of an item that renders it a tereifa; Rava says, in the case of an item that renders it a carcass; Rav Sheshet says, in the case of an item without which it dies; each Sage adds to his fellow’s. In the same way it is reasonable [to read] here: Rav Huna says its ear, Rav Ḥisda adds a tereifa, Rava adds a carcass. Similarly in chapter HaMapelet (Niddah 23b), regarding a body that is sealed down to the knee, and one adds: down to its navel. As for Rava’s statement there [in Niddah] that if its gullet is perforated, its mother is impure with the impurity of childbirth: even if we read Rava in our passage after Rav Ḥisda, Rava does not contradict Rava there, for although a perforated gullet is a tereifa, they do not compare it to a deficiency down to the knee.
tosafot:a15.1: That of Rav Huna and Rav Ḥisda and Rava do not disagree: it is obvious that Rav Ḥisda and Rava disagree [with each other]. Rather, this is what it means: that of Rav Huna does not disagree with Rav Ḥisda and Rava.
tosafot:a17.1: What is different from non-viable newborns: even though there a verse is written [for non-viable newborns], we should have derived [our case] from there; or else derive non-viable newborns from partnership, since “all the firstborn” is written, and treat all the derashot alike.
gershom:a1.1: What, is it not: the clause “even though he is not permitted” refers to the animal, that one may not give it to him in receivership for half the offspring; and the same applies according to Rabbi Yehuda: one may not sell an animal for its fetuses.
gershom:a2.1: No, it refers to the fetus: he is not permitted because she is pregnant; when he gives her to him in receivership it is forbidden because of the fetus. But if she is not pregnant and he wishes to sell [her] for the fetus, we still do not know.
gershom:a3.1: The language is also precise, since it teaches “him” and “its value” [in the masculine]: learn from it that it refers to the fetus. In any event, one cannot learn from here, according to Rabbi Yehuda, whether one may sell an animal for its fetuses or not.
gershom:a4.1: That which it teaches “they penalize,” etc., supports Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish.
gershom:a5.1: That which it teaches “up to ten times its value”: is it specific, that if the gentile raises [the price] to ten times its value, they penalize him to pay up to ten times its value and redeem it? Or is ten not specific but merely an exaggeration, teaching us that he must redeem it even for more than it is worth, but not as much as ten?
gershom:a6.1: Up to one hundred times its value: since for a slave he states one hundred times more than its value, conclude that the ten stated for an animal is meant specifically; for if not, let him teach ten for a slave as well.
gershom:a7.1: Actually, for an animal it is not specific, and a slave is different. That is why he states one hundred, and not ten as well: for every day [the gentile] keeps him from the mitzvot once he has sold him to a gentile. Therefore we penalize him so.
gershom:a8.1: Some say that Reish Lakish said [up to one hundred] regarding an animal, and the whole matter is taught in another way.
gershom:a9.1: We learned, etc., up to ten times its value: a refutation of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish, who said up to one hundred.
gershom:a10.1: It is not difficult: for a sale we penalize him up to one hundred because it is cut off from him, for he sold it entirely.
gershom:a11.1: Receivership, etc.: therefore we penalize him up to ten, not more.
gershom:a12.1: Specifically or not specifically: that which it teaches, “up to one hundred times its value”: specifically, actually up to one hundred? Or not specifically, but an exaggeration: because he sold it, they penalize him more and more beyond its value, but not that much; and in receivership he pays more than its value, but not as much as one who sells.
gershom:a13.1: Up to ten times its value: in this version he teaches the statement of Rabbi Yehoshua [ben Levi] the other way around. Since he says ten times its value for a slave and one hundred for an animal, conclude that the hundred for an animal is not specific: if for a slave, whom [the gentile] keeps from the mitzvot every day, he says only ten times its value, all the more so for an animal. So conclude it is not specific.
gershom:a14.1: Actually it is meant specifically, for an animal [the text adds “impure”]. And for a slave he therefore says up to ten and no more, because a slave is different: he does not willingly return to his Israelite master, for once his master has sold him to a gentile he hates his master and does not want to return to him. Therefore we penalize his master no more than up to ten times his value. And we object: an animal, why do we say up to one hundred times its value? Because the animal returns to its master, since it does not care whether it goes back. If that is the reason, that an animal returns, why say up to one hundred? Let him be penalized to redeem it for one more than its value. Rather, that we say ten and no more for a slave is not because of returning; rather, it is uncommon for a person to sell his slave to a gentile, and in an uncommon matter the Sages did not decree. That is why they penalized only up to ten. An animal is commonly sold, and they decreed. And now one cannot say, “Let him be penalized one more for an animal,” since we no longer attribute the reason, for either a slave or an animal, to its returning.
gershom:a15.1: Sanctify to Me all the firstborn: [“firstborn”] implies part of a firstborn, that even if the Israelite owns a share not in all of it but in part of it, he is obligated to redeem it.
gershom:a16.1: Until all of it is there: unless the firstborn belongs entirely to the Israelite, he is not obligated.
gershom:a17.1: That even if he has any share at all in it, he is obligated.
gershom:a18.1: It implies the majority: that most of it belongs to the Israelite. The Rabbis hold that the “all” that is written comes to fill it out: unless it belongs entirely to the Israelite, he is not obligated.
gershom:a19.1: To detract: that even if any amount belongs to the Israelite, he is obligated.
gershom:a20.1: And let him say to the gentile: Take your ear and go, and give the firstborn to the priest; and if it is not fit for the altar, it is fit for the priest to eat. And this is difficult for Rav Huna.
gershom:a21.1: Rav Ḥisda says: if the gentile has a share in the firstborn in a limb that would render it a carcass were the gentile to take it while it is alive, for example the thigh together with its hollow [the hip socket], it is a carcass; even though it still convulses, it is a carcass, since it is considered as dead.
gershom:a22.1: And Rava says: even if he has a share in an item that would render it a tereifa were he to take his share, for example from the knee joint upward, it is exempt from firstborn status, since [the priest] cannot say to him, “Take your share and go,” for the rest is not fit. He holds that a tereifa does not live twelve months, and it is as though dead were he to take his share.
gershom:a23.1: They said it, etc.: Rav Ḥisda and Rava do not disagree with Rav Huna. What Rav Huna said, “even its ear,” he said of it, the firstborn itself; what Rav Ḥisda and Rava said is of its mother. Rav Huna holds like them regarding its mother, and they hold like him regarding it.
gershom:a24.1: Rav Pappa said to them: they certainly disagree. Rav Huna holds that its mother is like the offspring, and they hold that the offspring is like its mother. What is different about it, etc.
gershom:a25.1: Mar bar Rav Ashi objects: to all of them. Why does a gentile’s partnership in an item that renders it a tereifa or a carcass exempt it, unlike non-viable newborns, which, though not viable and full carcasses, are sanctified as firstborn and require burial?
gershom:a26.1: And from where do we know that they are sacred? It is written “that emerges from [sheger] an animal”: whatever comes out of the animal first, even a non-viable newborn, is sacred. There, with non-viable newborns, since nothing non-sacred is mixed in them, the gentile having no partnership in them, we call them “all the firstborn” of Israel, and they are sacred even as carcasses.
rashi:b1.1: This is what Rabbi Yoḥanan said: in the study hall: the “obligated” that it teaches means obligated to be given to the priest, but it is not offered on the altar, since the fact that it changed is a permanent blemish, for which one slaughters it outside, like a blemished firstborn that the priest slaughters and eats.
rashi:b1.2: Even a slight blemish: even if the gentile has a partnership only in its ear, so that were he to take his share it would be neither a carcass nor a tereifa but merely a slight blemish, it is exempt from firstborn status.
rashi:b2.1: In accordance with Rav Huna: who said even its ear.
rashi:b3.1: We learned: below, in the chapter Al Elu Mumin (40a).
rashi:b4.1: Here it changed, etc.: and that is why Rabbi Yoḥanan needed to teach us that it is a blemish.
rashi:b4.2: Or one large: like a calf’s, or one small, like a goose’s.
rashi:b5.1: There is sanctity of the firstborn in its species: and even so it is a blemish. So why did Rabbi Yoḥanan need to say it?
rashi:b6.1: No, because it is sarua: the sarua stated in the Torah is one with one limb larger than its counterpart. But of another change, for example its wool resembling a goat’s, we have not heard that it is a blemish; therefore Rabbi Yoḥanan needed to teach it to us.
rashi:b6.2: These blemishes: that the Sages explained regarding a firstborn.
rashi:b6.3: Whether transient or permanent, they disqualify: in a person, that is, in a priest; as long as the blemish is on him, he may not perform the service.
rashi:b7.1: Equal to his seed: one who looks like other people.
rashi:b9.1: Actually I will say to you, etc.: and from here it is not reasonable [to say that it is] because of sarua.
rashi:b9.2: Both should have been: and this one is certainly a deviation. And if you ask why Rabbi Yoḥanan needed to say it, since we have established that a change is a blemish, the answer is: since one could also say that it is not due to the change but due to sarua, Rabbi Yoḥanan needed to say it.
rashi:b10.2: She came before Rava: to ask whether they are obligated in firstborn status.
rashi:b11.1: He would transfer their ears to a gentile: to exempt them from firstborn status.
rashi:b11.2: And he prohibited them: the firstborns, from shearing and labor like full firstborns, and he gave them to the priests.
rashi:b11.3: And the animals came to an end: his livestock died.
rashi:b12.1: Into a mishap: lest they shear them or work them.
rashi:b12.2: If so: since he intended it for good, why did his animals come to an end?
rashi:b13.1: Before it emerges: and it is not yet sanctified, for the sanctity of a firstborn depends on the womb, as it is written “every firstborn that is born” (Deuteronomy 15:19); so this is not like inflicting a blemish on consecrated animals.
rashi:b13.2: He does not abrogate the sanctity of the priest: for it is like a blemished firstborn, which is given to the priest, and the priest must treat it with sanctity: he may not shear it or work it, and when he slaughters it he does not slaughter it in the butcher’s market, nor is it sold in the market or weighed by the litra, as below (31a).
rashi:b13.3: Here: once he transfers it to the gentile, no status of sanctity takes effect on it; and even though he treats it with sanctity, it is like treating fully non-sacred animals with sanctity.
rashi:b14.1: A complete transaction: to take money from the gentile, for a gentile acquires only with money, as we say below in the second chapter (13a).
rashi:b14.2: Performed a matter: merely a matter of words, without taking payment.
rashi:b15.1: Mishna: Priests and Levites are exempt: it now enters your mind that it refers to the firstborn of a donkey.
rashi:b15.2: If they rendered exempt: the Levites [exempted] the firstborn of Israel in the wilderness.
rashi:b15.3: It is logical, etc.: and this implies that the Levites themselves exempted the Israelites’ donkeys.
tosafot:b8.1: Rather, is it not because it is sarua: and a change is not a blemish. And if you say: if so, it is all the more difficult for Rabbi Yoḥanan, who said above that since it changed it is a blemish, for here we infer that two large eyes are a change and yet not considered a blemish? One can say: the change above is more severe than two large eyes or two small ones.
tosafot:b12.1: In brief: Because he abrogated their sanctity: this bears on why we are not careful about this nowadays, even though Rav Mari was punished. Rabbeinu Tam explained that Rav Mari was punished because he transferred the ear of the fetus, so the abrogation was in the body of the fetus itself; but transferring [a share] in the mother is permitted. Some books read “her ears” in the feminine, but that refers to the flock; so too “he prohibited her from shearing and labor.” Question: below (53a), on why animal tithe is not practiced nowadays lest it lead to a mishap, the Gemara asks: then the firstborn too should not be practiced nowadays, and answers that it is possible [to avoid a mishap] as Rav Yehuda says [by blemishing it before birth]. Why not find a remedy through the mothers, as explained? Answer: there, since one could avoid the mishap without abrogating the priest’s sanctity by following Rav Yehuda, they did not want to establish a permanent remedy by abrogation; but if one did it, it is done. Alternatively: in Rav Mari’s day people were expert in blemishing a firstborn before it emerged, so it was forbidden to use abrogation; but we, who are not expert in this, had better transfer to a gentile before coming to a mishap, as is implied below (53a): were it not possible as Rav Yehuda says, we would institute transferring to gentiles, and for us, who are not expert, it is as if it were not possible. [A parenthetical adds that even Rav Yehuda’s method might be forbidden as a precaution, lest the fetus put out its head before the blemish is made, were it not preferable to waiting for a blemish to occur on its own.] It seems that transferring the ear alone is permitted, since we hold like Rav Huna, as Rabbi Yoḥanan stands with him and said “even a slight blemish”; and Rav Mari, who transferred their ears, was punished only for the abrogation. Below (53a) it asks, “let him transfer their ears to a gentile”; and at most it is permitted by transferring an item that renders it a tereifa or a carcass. According to the other version, that Rav Mari was punished because he knew how to transfer properly while others did not and thought he had done a mere matter of words, one may also explain that Rav Mari, who was expert in Rav Yehuda’s method, should not have used an acquisition, since others would come to err; but for us there is no other way. Rabbeinu Tam further explained: for Rav Mari to transfer the fetus’s ear to a gentile would be transferring something not yet in the world; rather, he transferred the animal for the ears of the fetus, like a palm tree for its fruit, and people would err and think he transferred the fetus’s ears like the fruit of a palm, and come to a mishap; but transferring the animals’ own ears is permitted, since no one would err. According to Rashi’s explanation this cannot be said, for he explained that Rav Mari knew how to make a complete acquisition by taking money from the gentile, since a gentile acquires only with money (13a), while others thought he did a mere matter of words without taking payment. But by his own words he should not have cited proof from below; on the contrary, according to Rabbi Yoḥanan, who said that by Torah law money effects acquisition, it is expounded below (13b): “from the hand of your fellow” [one acquires] with money, but from a gentile by pulling, and we hold like Rabbi Yoḥanan. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:b15.1: Priests and Levites exempted themselves by an a fortiori inference: And if you say: even without the a fortiori, derive it from the answer the Gemara gives below (5b) to the officer Controcus: those three hundred [Levites] were firstborn, and a firstborn does not cancel a firstborn, for it is enough that it cancels its own [sanctity]; learn from this that it at least cancels its own. One can say: were it not for the a fortiori, we could answer that those three hundred were firstborn and needed redemption. And if you say: if so, let them be counted with the two hundred seventy-three who were left over, one could say that Scripture undertook to count only the Israelites by themselves.
gershom:b1.1: This is what Rabbi Yoḥanan said: even a slight blemish, like Rav Huna, who said that even [if the gentile owns] its ear, it is exempt. And this too was said in the study hall: as we learned, “A ewe that gave birth,” etc., is exempt from the firstborn, as it is written “the firstborn of a goat” (Numbers 18:17): only when it and its firstborn are goats.
gershom:b2.1: And if it has some features resembling its mother, it is obligated in firstborn status. And this is the novelty said in the study hall: that this lookalike is a permanent blemish, even though it has some features [of its mother]; it is slaughtered on account of this blemish and is disqualified for the altar.
gershom:b3.1: And Rabbi Elazar said to him: Granted, the slight blemish he mentioned is a novelty, for it teaches us that we say even its ear.
gershom:b4.1: And if you would say: this is a blemish because it changed into something whose species is not sanctified as a firstborn, a pig.
gershom:b5.1: Here: with the ewe that gave birth, it changed into something whose species is sanctified as a firstborn, and even so it is a blemish; and that is his novelty.
gershom:b6.1: This too we learned: that it is a blemish.
gershom:b7.1: No: we do not learn it from here, for here it is a blemish not because of the change; rather, when its eye is as large as a calf’s, that is a full blemish, namely sarua, and we say that anything extra is as though missing. Had it not been said in the study hall that a change is a permanent blemish, we would not learn it from here, since this is sarua.
gershom:b8.1: So too it stands to reason: that this is because of sarua and not because of the change.
gershom:b9.1: As we learned: these blemishes, which it lists there.
gershom:b10.1: No, actually I will say to you: a change is a blemish, and we learn it from here.
gershom:b11.1: And that which is difficult for you: if it is because of the change, then even if both are large too.
gershom:b12.1: There: both large or both small is not because of a change; either both are large from extra health, or they are small from weakness. But here, with one large and one small, it is neither from health nor from weakness but from a change. So we still learn it from here, and the question returns to its place.
gershom:b13.1: Her gentile brothers would give her animals to fatten from her own [resources], so that half would belong to each.
gershom:b14.1: She came before Rava: and he exempted her from the firstborn.
gershom:b15.1: Had a certain ḥeivata: a herd of animals.
gershom:b16.1: He would transfer their ears: of his firstborns, in their mothers’ wombs, to a gentile, for after they were born he could not transfer them, [since] the priest [had acquired them], for coming out of the womb sanctifies. And he did not mean to exempt them from the firstborn, for even so he prohibited them from shearing and labor and gave them to the priests; rather, so that if an Israelite did not know it was a firstborn and slaughtered it and ate it, he would not come to a mishap, since it would be non-sacred.
gershom:b17.1: And the animals came to an end: his animals died because he was taking them out to non-sacred status.
gershom:b18.1: If so: since his intention was good, why did the animals die? Because, etc.
gershom:b19.1: It is permitted to inflict a blemish on a firstborn: so as not to come to a mishap with it.
gershom:b20.1: Before it emerges into the air of the world: for after it has fully emerged it is forbidden. [An editor’s note in the printed text suggests reading: And likewise one could transfer it to a gentile then; so why did Rav Mari’s animals die? The printed words that follow, “they thus to the Israelite, of Rav Mari,” appear garbled.]
gershom:b21.1: There: in Rav Yehuda’s case, it is permitted because he abrogates only the sanctity of the altar.
gershom:b22.1: And if you wish, say Rav Mari too [an editor’s note in the printed text suggests: Rav Mari too, though he abrogated even the priest’s sanctity, it is permitted, since partnership with a gentile is exempt, etc.] abrogated the priest’s sanctity from them, since partnership with a gentile is exempt. And this is why Rav Mari bar Raḥel’s animals died: he knew how to transfer them with a complete acquisition, valid for anyone even in his absence, for example through his adult son and daughter, who have legal capacity and acquired it for the gentile with a full acquisition, so that the gentile has a share in it. But not everyone knows this, since they have not learned [the law]; one who saw Rav Mari transferring to a gentile would go and transfer too, thinking he could do it even through his minor son and daughter, and would do it through them, treat the animals as non-sacred and come to a mishap. That is why his animals died: through him others stumbled.
gershom:b23.1: The priests and the Levites are exempt: from redeeming their firstborn donkeys, by an a fortiori inference: if they exempted, etc.
gershom:b24.1: It now enters our mind that we are speaking of the Levites themselves: if they exempted the Israelites’ firstborn donkeys in the wilderness, as it is written, “Take the Levites in place of every firstborn,” etc., it is logical that they should exempt their own firstborn donkeys. And the Gemara wonders [on 4a]: did the Levites themselves exempt the firstborn donkeys in the wilderness?
